lesson.title: Energy in the Magnetic Field: What an Inductor Holds
lesson.summary: An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field created by current flowing through its coil, following E equals one half L I squared, the magnetic mirror of a capacitor's energy formula.
lesson.body:
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field built from separated charge. An inductor, its magnetic counterpart, stores energy in a magnetic field built from current flowing through its coiled wire, exactly the coil-and-current relationship you just saw create a concentrated magnetic field. Where a capacitor resists a change in voltage, an inductor resists a change in current, generating a back voltage across itself, described by V equals L times the rate of change of current, whenever that current tries to ramp up or down. Building current through an inductor from zero up to some final value I means pushing against that opposing voltage the whole way, and the work spent doing that pushing is stored in the resulting magnetic field.

The energy formula follows the same logical shape as the capacitor's. Early in the ramp, current is low, so the opposing back voltage is small and little work is needed to nudge current up further. As current climbs, the opposition grows, so later increments of current cost more work than earlier ones. Working through that relationship the same way as for the capacitor, current standing in for voltage and inductance standing in for capacitance, gives the energy stored in an inductor as E equals one half times L times I squared, with E in joules, L in henries, and I in amperes.

Apply it to a 100 millihenry inductor, written as 0.1 henries, carrying a steady 2 amps, a reasonable pairing for a coil found in a small power converter. First square the current: 2 squared is 4. Multiply by the inductance: 0.1 times 4 equals 0.4. Take half of that: 0.4 divided by 2 equals 0.2 joules stored in the magnetic field surrounding that coil while 2 amps flows through it.

Notice how closely this mirrors the capacitor's E equals one half C V squared, with the roles of the two key quantities swapped: a capacitor's stored energy depends on the voltage across it and its capacitance, while an inductor's stored energy depends on the current through it and its inductance. This symmetry has a sharp practical consequence. Just as a charged capacitor holds its voltage until given a discharge path, a current carrying inductor holds its current and fights to keep it flowing. Break that current path suddenly, say by opening a switch feeding a relay coil, and the inductor's stored magnetic energy has to go somewhere in an instant, producing a brief but often very high voltage spike across the opening contacts, which is exactly why relay and motor circuits typically include a flyback diode to give that stored energy a safe path to dissipate.

Far from being just a nuisance to manage, this same energy storage mechanism is put to deliberate use in switching power supplies, where an inductor is charged with energy from the source during part of each switching cycle and then discharges that stored energy into the output during the rest of the cycle, converting one voltage level to another far more efficiently than a purely resistive approach ever could.
